clue.text: Cavalryman in a shipwreck

indicators.note: to wreck something is to smash it up, so the letters of the words before it are broken and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A horse soldier is caught up in a disaster at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shipwreck' reads as one word, but it splits: the letters of A SHIP are rearranged, with 'wreck' as the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A spahi was a soldier in the Turkish or French Algerian mounted troops, so a horse soldier.

clue.text: Clement-this old leader in battle, effectively…

indicators.note: the word in tells us the name sits inside the following words, spanning their join

explanation.surface: A gentle old commander proves effective in combat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clement' looks like the adjective meaning mild; it is a first name, and the leader's surname runs across BATTLE and EFFECTIVELY.
explanation.definitionFit: Clement Attlee was the British Labour prime minister from 1945 to 1951.

clue.text: … and in forming a cabinet, he moved no hearts

indicators.note: letters that are moved are shifted into a new order, so the fodder beside this word is rearranged

explanation.surface: A party leader puts a government together without compassion, discarding the soft-hearted.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries on from the previous clue's political scene, so 'cabinet' suggests ministers; here it is furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Sheraton was an eighteenth-century English furniture designer known for cabinets and chairs.

clue.text: Poison-champion on it internally

indicators.note: something held internally sits inside, so the second piece goes within the first

parts.note: an ace is a champion or expert
taken as written, both words joined

explanation.surface: A poison is administered to the winner from within.
explanation.definitionFit: Monkshood, a plant whose root is highly toxic, is also called by this name.

clue.text: Fell-race competitor who never wins

explanation.definitionFit: Someone racing up a fell (a hill in northern England) runs uphill; the second-placed finisher in any contest is by definition not the winner.

clue.text: Tells all about the Camptown reporters?

parts.note: the song Camptown Races is sung in dialect, with de standing for the
scribes are writers, here journalists

explanation.surface: Someone recounts the doings of the journalists in a small American town.
explanation.walkthrough: Camptown Races is a minstrel song whose lyric begins 'De Camptown ladies sing dis song', so 'the Camptown' word is DE.
explanation.definitionFit: To describe something is to give a full account of it.

clue.text: Dermatologist's examination without appointment?

explanation.definitionFit: A skin doctor would literally check spots on the skin; a random inspection made without warning or arrangement is the everyday sense.

clue.text: Gold study of poet

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a den is a private room for work or study

explanation.surface: A golden piece of work about a poet.
explanation.definitionFit: W. H. Auden was an Anglo-American poet of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Common complaint of worker fellow

parts.note: a worker is a bee, in crossword convention

explanation.surface: An ordinary grievance raised by a colleague at work.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a grumble or grievance, a usage common in informal speech.

clue.text: Issue in which rich lend abnormally

indicators.note: behaving abnormally means out of the usual order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A situation where wealthy people make loans in an unusual way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' is a legal word for offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue means a person's offspring, sons and daughters.

clue.text: English university pleasant for a girl?

parts.note: nice means pleasant or agreeable

explanation.surface: An agreeable English college might suit a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A female first name, and the question mark admits it is just one example.

clue.text: Mountain-top has no work for the crooked

parts.note: ben is a Scottish word for a mountain, as in Ben Nevis

indicators.note: something that has no part of itself loses it, so the following word is taken out

parts.note: taken as written
op, short for opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: A summit offers no employment for dishonest people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mountain-top' reads as one thing; split it into BEN and TOP, then remove OP from TOP to leave T.
explanation.definitionFit: Bent is slang for dishonest or corrupt, as crooked also means.

clue.text: Stern bar is hard lines on Welshman

indicators.note: in an across answer, putting one piece on another places it after

parts.note: Taff is a nickname for a man from Wales
a rail is a solid metal line, as in a railway track

explanation.surface: Tough luck is dealt out to a man from Wales who is severe at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard lines' pretends to be the British phrase for bad luck; here it means rails. 'Stern' is the back of a ship, not severe.
explanation.definitionFit: The handrail round a ship's after deck, so a barrier at the back of the vessel.

clue.text: Ruthlessly ambitious sort finds way in Riviera resort

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation for way inside the rearranged letters
to re-sort is to sort again, so the letters of the place name are put in a new order

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A pushy social climber turns up in a fashionable Mediterranean holiday town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' looks like a holiday town but is RE-SORT, rearranging RIVIERA, and ST goes inside that.
explanation.definitionFit: An arriviste is an upstart who has recently gained status and is aggressively self-seeking.

clue.text: Robber needs equipment in Ali Baba's gang

indicators.note: in places the word for equipment inside the word for the gang

parts.note: the forty thieves of Ali Baba's tale form a band
a rig is a set of gear or equipment

explanation.surface: A thief needs his kit among the forty thieves of the old story.
explanation.definitionFit: A brigand is a bandit who robs travellers, so a thief.

clue.text: Happy I find oil-change bloomers

parts.note: glad means happy

indicators.note: a change of these letters puts them in a different order

explanation.surface: A cheerful person discovers that swapping engine fluid is a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomers' suggests mistakes or underwear; it means flowers that bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: These are flowering plants grown for their tall spikes of blooms.

clue.text: This short verse of Twain needs time

parts.note: twain is an old word for two, a couple

explanation.surface: A brief poem by Mark Twain requires time to compose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twain' looks like Mark Twain the author; it is the archaic word for two.
explanation.definitionFit: A pair of rhyming lines of verse, so a very short poem.

clue.text: Healing preparation from date, with loose pap removed

indicators.note: letters removed are taken away from the longer word

parts.note: a date is an arranged meeting or engagement
pap set loose is jumbled, giving its three letters in another order

explanation.surface: A soothing balm made from a fruit after the soft mush is taken out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'date' suggests the fruit but is an engagement; 'loose' rearranges PAP to APP, which comes off the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A salve or cream rubbed on the skin to soothe or heal.

clue.text: Hellish end of predatory giants, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps signals that a different arrangement of these letters is meant
the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A fearsome final scene in which monsters prey on their victims.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to the Styx, the river of the underworld in Greek myth, hence dark and infernal.

clue.text: It ties dressing round pheasant for instance

indicators.note: putting one thing round another places the second inside the first

parts.note: lint is a fabric used for dressing wounds
pheasant is an example of game birds

explanation.surface: A cook bandages a bird for roasting with string.
explanation.definitionFit: A band of tough tissue that binds bones together at a joint.

clue.text: For example, Gilbert and Sullivan can make souffles

parts.note: G and S are the initials of the operetta duo

explanation.surface: The comic opera duo, say, are able to cook up light dishes.
explanation.definitionFit: Beaten whites and yolks are the essential ingredient of a soufflé.

clue.text: Name given to mimic showing some neck

parts.note: to ape is to mimic or copy

explanation.surface: A named impersonator shows a little cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some neck' looks like impudence; it is part of the neck.
explanation.definitionFit: The back part of the neck, so a section of it.

clue.text: Self-raising explosive device?

parts.note: from Hamlet's phrase about the engineer hoist with his own bomb, blown up by the device he set

explanation.definitionFit: An early bomb for blasting gates; being 'hoist with one's own' means hurt by one's own scheme.

clue.text: Off-chance at Lord's?

parts.note: in cricket a faint edge off the bat, often to the off side, can give the fielders a catching chance

explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the London cricket ground; 'off' is the side of the field a batsman faces.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, a slight deflection of the ball off the edge of the bat.

clue.text: Rambling, I take family into Dad's Army

indicators.note: putting pieces into another places them inside it

parts.note: the Home Guard, abbreviated HG, was nicknamed Dad's Army
kin means family or relatives

explanation.surface: A rambling story in which I bring my relatives into a classic TV comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: Dad's Army is a British TV sitcom about the wartime Home Guard (HG), the volunteer force of older men.
explanation.definitionFit: Walking for pleasure in the countryside, so going on a long walk.

clue.text: Garnet, say, — old comic carrying some weight

parts.note: The Gem was a British boys' story paper of the early twentieth century
a stone is a British unit of weight of fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: A veteran comedian named Garnet is carrying a little extra weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Garnet' looks like a first name; it is the red mineral.
explanation.definitionFit: A garnet is an example of a precious or semi-precious mineral used in jewellery.

clue.text: Bird with a wooden leg

explanation.definitionFit: A long-legged wading bird; also a pole with a footrest for walking raised off the ground.

clue.text: Principle pair spliced on board

parts.note: main means principal, chief; the clue spells it principle
a brace is a pair, as of game birds

explanation.surface: The chief couple are joined together on a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'splice the mainbrace' is the naval order to issue an extra ration of rum; the mainbrace is a rope on the mainmast yard.
explanation.definitionFit: The rope traditionally spliced on a sailing ship, giving the naval phrase for a celebratory tot of rum.
